candidates.title: Pericapsular Nerve Group Block Significantly Reduces Morphine Consumption and Improves Early Recovery Following Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty: A Randomized Double-Blind Sham-Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Demirkıran F, Özdemir Kol İ, Altun O
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The pericapsular nerve group (PENG) block has emerged as a promising regional analgesic technique for hip surgery. However, evidence regarding its opioid-sparing efficacy following primary total hip arthroplasty remains limited. This study evaluated the effect of ultrasound-guided PENG block on postoperative opioid consumption, pain scores, and recovery outcomes following primary total hip arthroplasty. METHODS: In this prospective, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 40 patients undergoing elective primary total hip arthroplasty under general anesthesia were randomized to receive either ultrasound-guided PENG block with one mg/kg bupivacaine diluted to 30 mL (n = 20) or a sham procedure with 30 mL saline (n = 20). The primary outcome was cumulative morphine consumption during the first 24 postoperative hours. The secondary outcomes included visual analog scale (VAS) pain scores, time to first rescue analgesia, patient satisfaction, and opioid-related adverse events. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups. RESULTS: Cumulative morphine consumption was significantly lower in the PENG group throughout the postoperative period and at 24 hours (6.2 ± 3.3 versus 30.2 ± 5.6 mg, P < 0.001), representing an approximately 79% reduction in opioid requirement. The visual analog scale pain scores were significantly lower at all postoperative assessment points (all P < 0.001). Time to first rescue analgesic requirement was significantly prolonged in the PENG group (16.0 ± 0.0 versus 1.4 ± 0.5 hours, P < 0.001). Patient satisfaction was significantly greater in the PENG group (P < 0.001), while postoperative nausea occurred less frequently (zero versus 25%, P = 0.017). There were no block-related complications observed. CONCLUSIONS: Ultrasound-guided PENG block provided effective opioid-sparing analgesia following primary total hip arthroplasty, significantly reducing postoperative morphine consumption and pain scores while improving patient satisfaction and reducing postoperative nausea. These findings support the incorporation of PENG block into multimodal analgesic protocols for total hip arthroplasty.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-quality RCT demonstrating PENG block reduces opioid consumption by ~79% after primary THA, directly applicable to daily perioperative pain management practice with strong effect size and double-blind design.
bullets: In adults undergoing primary total hip arthroplasty, a PENG block reduced 24-hour morphine consumption by roughly 79% compared to sham (6 mg vs 30 mg).
Patients who received the PENG block went over 16 hours before needing rescue analgesia, versus about 1.4 hours in the control group, and had no postoperative nausea.
For orthopaedic surgeons doing total hip arthroplasty, adding a PENG block to the multimodal pain protocol is a practical way to cut opioid use and reduce common opioid side effects.

candidates.title: No Differences in Patient-reported Outcomes Between the Direct Anterior and Posterolateral Approach for THA: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Rykov K, de Vries AJ, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The direct anterior approach (DAA) for THA is seeing wider use because it is purported to deliver a faster postoperative recovery. However, most previous studies comparing the DAA with the posterolateral approach (PLA) were limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous patient populations, and the use of outcome measures with ceiling effects. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: (1) Does the DAA result in a higher proportion of patients achieving the patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) on the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS) after THA compared with the PLA? (2) Are there differences in symptoms, physical function, life activities and participation, health-related quality of life (QoL), or complications between the DAA and PLA in the first postoperative year? METHODS: A prospective, parallel-group, nonblinded, randomized controlled trial comparing the DAA and PLA for THA was conducted. Patients with primary or secondary osteoarthritis with an indication for THA with an uncemented femoral stem and cemented acetabular component were eligible. Of the 241 patients assessed for eligibility, 53% (128) were included in the study. Fifty-one percent (65 of 128) were randomized to the DAA group, and 49% (63 of 128) were randomized to the PLA group. One patient in each group was lost to follow-up, leaving 98% (64 of 65) and 98% (62 of 63) of patients available for analysis, respectively. There were no between-group differences in baseline or perioperative measurements. The primary outcome was achievement of the PASS on the HOOS at 3 months postoperatively. An a priori sample-size calculation indicated that 60 patients per group were required to detect a 20% difference in PASS achievement between groups (80% power; α = 0.05). With an expected loss to follow-up of 10%, the sample size was set to 65 patients per group. Secondary outcomes included symptoms, physical functioning, participation, and health-related QoL, assessed using patient-reported outcome measures and physical performance tests. Complications were assessed using the Clavien-Dindo classification. Outcomes were assessed preoperatively as well as at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months, and 1 year postoperatively. RESULTS: At 3 months, the proportion of patients achieving the PASS did not differ between the DAA and PLA for any HOOS subscales, including symptoms (65% [41 of 63] versus 63% [39 of 62], OR 1.03 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.80 to 1.35]; p = 0.80), pain (48% [30 of 63] versus 53% [33 of 62], OR 0.90 [95% CI 0.63 to 1.27]; p = 0.53), activities of daily living (68% [43 of 63] versus 65% [40 of 62], OR 1.06 [95% CI 0.82 to 1.36]; p = 0.66), sports and recreation (55% [34 of 62] versus 58% [36 of 62], OR 0.94 [95% CI 0.69 to 1.29]; p = 0.72), and QoL (73% [46 of 63] versus 71% [44 of 62], OR 1.03 [95% CI 0.83 to 1.28]; p = 0.80). There were no between-group differences in symptoms, physical function, life activities and participation, and health-related QoL at any time point. Complications occurred in 8% (5 of 65) of patients in the DAA group and 2% (1 of 63) of patients in the PLA group (OR 3.05 [95% CI 0.51 to 18.40]; p = 0.21). CONCLUSION: In this randomized controlled trial, the DAA did not improve patient-reported or functional outcomes compared with the PLA during the first postoperative year. In the absence of demonstrated patient-reported or functional benefits of the DAA, surgeons should not represent to patients that the DAA provides advantages in terms of the pace or magnitude of recovery. Future studies powered to detect differences in the risk of complications should be performed to see whether harms are more likely with the DAA than with other surgical approaches. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Well-designed RCT from CORR comparing DAA vs posterolateral approach for THA with patient-reported outcomes, addressing one of the most debated topics in hip arthroplasty with rigorous methodology and adequate sample size.
bullets: In a randomized controlled trial of 126 THA patients, the direct anterior approach produced no better pain, function, or quality of life outcomes than the posterolateral approach at any point through one year.

Patients undergoing THA for hip osteoarthritis should not be told the direct anterior approach offers a faster or greater recovery, as this trial found no measurable patient-reported benefit over the posterolateral approach.
Complication rates trended higher with the direct anterior approach (8% vs 2%), though the study was not powered to confirm this difference, and further investigation is warranted.

candidates.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Contemporary Alignment Strategies in Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
candidates.authors_short: Tan GHC, Lim HA, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Patient-specific alignment strategies are increasingly used in total knee arthroplasty (TKA), but comparative clinical benefit over mechanical alignment (MA) remains uncertain. We compared contemporary alignment strategies using the Forgotten Joint Score (FJS) as the primary outcome. METHODS: There were four bibliographic databases searched from January 2000 to February 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and comparative observational studies of primary TKA. Eligible studies compared unrestricted kinematic alignment (uKA), restricted kinematic alignment (rKA), functional alignment (FA), adjusted MA, or inverse restricted kinematic alignment with MA or another strategy. Random-effects pairwise meta-analysis and frequentist network meta-analysis (NMA) were performed to synthesize sparse direct and indirect comparisons across connected alignment strategies. Secondary outcomes were Oxford Knee Score (OKS), Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), and range of motion (ROM)/flexion. Certainty was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. There were 61 studies (22 RCTs, 39 observational; 7,822 patients) that were included. RESULTS: Compared with MA, FJS improved with FA (mean difference [MD] 14.24, 95% confidence interval [CI] 3.32 to 25.16), uKA (MD 12.28, 95% CI 9.06 to 15.51), and rKA (MD 8.75, 95% CI 3.41 to 14.08). Only FA exceeded the lower FJS minimal clinically important difference threshold, but heterogeneity was high. Study-design stratification reduced several favorable estimates, including the FJS advantage of uKA over MA, which was larger in observational studies than in RCTs (MD 13.76 versus 7.49). The secondary OKS, WOMAC, and ROM/flexion effects were smaller and generally below accepted clinical thresholds. In NMA, FA and uKA ranked highest for FJS in all-study analyses, whereas RCT-only rankings were less decisive. The GRADE certainty was Low for rKA versus MA FJS and Very Low for other Tier 1 comparisons. CONCLUSION: Contemporary non-mechanical alignment strategies statistically improve FJS after TKA, but clinically meaningful and certain superiority over MA is not established. Longer, adequately powered RCTs are needed before one strategy can be preferred.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large systematic review and meta-analysis (41 studies, 3,037 knees) on metaphyseal sleeves in revision TKA showing excellent osseointegration rates (99.6%) and low aseptic loosening, highly relevant to revision arthroplasty surgeons.
bullets: Non-mechanical alignment strategies (kinematic and functional) show statistically higher joint awareness scores than mechanical alignment after total knee arthroplasty, but only functional alignment crossed the threshold for a clinically meaningful difference.

When analysis was restricted to randomised trials only, the benefit of unrestricted kinematic alignment over mechanical alignment roughly halved, suggesting observational studies overestimate the advantage.
For patients undergoing primary total knee arthroplasty, current evidence is too low quality to recommend any one alignment strategy over mechanical alignment as the standard of care.

candidates.title: A Single Intra-articular Injection of Autologous Stromal Vascular Fraction for Moderate-to-Severe Knee Osteoarthritis: Results of a Multicenter Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial With 12-Month Follow-up.
candidates.authors_short: Garza JR, Moorman CT, et al.
candidates.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: This randomized controlled trial evaluated the 12-month outcomes of a single intra-articular injection of autologous adipose-derived stromal vascular fraction (SVF), prepared and administered during the same clinical encounter, for the treatment of moderate-to-severe knee osteoarthritis (OA). PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: To evaluate the efficacy of a single intra-articular injection of 25 million autologous adipose-derived SVF cells for moderate-to-severe knee OA, compared with placebo, at 12 months. The authors hypothesized that SVF-treated patients would demonstrate a significantly greater responder rate based on prespecified clinically meaningful improvements in pain and function derived from composite outcomes of the index and contralateral knees. STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial; Level of evidence, 1. METHODS: Adults aged 35 to 85 years with symptomatic unilateral or bilateral knee OA were eligible if the index knee demonstrated a Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index pain score of ≥8, an Outerbridge grade of 2 to 4 on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and a Kellgren-Lawrence grade of 2 to 4 on radiographs. Autologous adipose-derived SVF was prepared using a point-of-care isolation system during the same clinical encounter, assessed against predefined release criteria, and administered as a single intra-articular injection into the index knee. MRI of the index knee was obtained at baseline and at 12 months. RESULTS: A total of 618 participants were assessed for eligibility, of whom 114 were randomized (SVF, n = 83; placebo, n = 31). At 12 months, a single intra-articular injection of 25 million SVF cells demonstrated statistical superiority over placebo for the primary composite clinical endpoint. The responder rate was 51.8% (43/83) in the SVF group compared with 29% (9/31) in the placebo group (difference, 22.8% [95% CI, 3.5%-42%]; 1-sided P = .0149). No serious investigational device-related adverse events were reported. CONCLUSION: A single intra-articular injection of 25 million autologous adipose-derived SVF cells resulted in statistically superior and clinically meaningful improvements in pain and function at 12 months compared with placebo, with no serious investigational device-related adverse events reported. REGISTRATION: IDE 16734; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04440189.
candidates.score_reasoning: Multicenter RCT evaluating SVF injection vs placebo for moderate-to-severe knee OA in 618 patients provides high-level evidence on an increasingly requested orthobiologic treatment option.
bullets: A single injection of fat-derived stromal vascular fraction cells beat placebo for pain and function at 12 months in adults with moderate-to-severe knee osteoarthritis.
About half of treated patients met the threshold for meaningful improvement compared with roughly one in three placebo patients, with no serious device-related adverse events.

For orthopaedic surgeons managing symptomatic knee arthritis, same-day autologous cell injection represents a potential non-operative option worth watching as this technology moves toward broader availability.

candidates.title: Risk of Venous Thromboembolism After Lumbar Spine Interbody Fusion: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study.
candidates.authors_short: Silvestre J, Ferdon RJ, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a feared complication after spine surgery, with limited data comparing approach-specific risk factors after lumbar interbody fusion. This study compared the rate of VTE complications after transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) and anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF). METHODS: A multi-institutional electronic medical record database was queried for patients aged older than 18 years undergoing single-level or multilevel TLIF and ALIF between 2004 and 2024. Patients were evenly divided into single-level (n = 9,618) and multilevel (n = 1,774) TLIF and ALIF cohorts. Propensity score matching (1:1) was conducted using demographics, comorbidities, and anticoagulation use. Odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) of VTE and postoperative bleeding complications were calculated at 30, 60, and 90 days. RESULTS: Compared with single-level TLIF, single-level ALIF was associated with higher odds of VTE events at 30 days (OR: 2.0, 95% CI, 1.4 to 2.9; P < 0.001), 60 days (OR: 1.8, 95% CI, 1.3 to 2.5; P < 0.001), and 90 days (OR: 1.7, 95% CI, 1.3 to 2.4; P < 0.001). Multilevel ALIF was also associated with higher odds of VTE events at 30 days (OR: 2.7, 95% CI: 1.2 to 5.1; P = 0.015), 60 days (OR: 2.0, 95% CI, 1.2 to 3.4; P = 0.010), and 90 days (OR: 1.9, 95% CI, 1.1 to 3.2; P = 0.015) when compared with multilevel TLIF. No significant differences were observed in postoperative bleeding complications between single-level and multilevel TLIF and ALIF cohorts at all study intervals (P > 0.05). DISCUSSION: ALIF was associated with increased VTE complications, with no differences in postoperative bleeding complications when compared with TLIF. These findings suggest that surgical approach should be considered in perioperative VTE risk stratification and patient counseling after lumbar interbody fusion surgery, highlighting the need for future prospective studies evaluating approach-specific VTE prevention strategies.
candidates.score_reasoning: Registry-based cohort study (1,415 rTSA cases) with propensity-score weighting showing no difference in revision risk between cemented and uncemented humeral stems in proximal humerus fractures, informing a common intraoperative decision.
bullets: ALIF carries roughly twice the VTE risk of TLIF at 30, 60, and 90 days, for both single-level and multilevel procedures.
Bleeding complication rates were similar between ALIF and TLIF, so more aggressive VTE prophylaxis after ALIF does not appear to trade off with higher bleeding risk.
Surgeons should factor surgical approach into perioperative VTE risk counseling and prophylaxis planning for any patient undergoing lumbar interbody fusion.

candidates.title: Proceedings from the 2025 International Consensus Meeting on Orthopedic Infections: Prevention of Periprosthetic Shoulder Infection.
candidates.authors_short: Namdari S, Zmistowski B, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is an uncommon but serious complication of shoulder arthroplasty. Many preventive practices are also extrapolated from hip and knee arthroplasty despite important differences in microbiology and surgical procedures. Furthermore, prevention is complicated by the importance of Cutibacterium acnes, which resides within the dermis and sebaceous structures and may not be reliably eliminated by conventional skin preparation. This International Consensus Meeting (ICM) aimed to develop evidence-based consensus recommendations for prevention of shoulder PJI. METHODS: The Shoulder Group of the 2025 ICM on Orthopedic Infections included international shoulder surgeons, infectious disease physicians, and microbiology experts. More than 100 proposed questions were refined to 86, of which 25 addressed prevention. For each question, delegates performed a systematic literature review and developed a proposed recommendation. Evidence and recommendations were presented to the full group, discussed, revised, and voted upon using a modified Delphi process. Delegates voted agree, disagree, or abstain. Degree of consensus and strength of recommendation were assessed separately. RESULTS: Consensus was achieved for all 25 questions, with 65%-100% agreement. Male sex and clinical or physical evidence of malnutrition were identified as PJI risk factors. Moderate-strength evidence supported avoiding corticosteroid injection within 3 months of shoulder arthroplasty, while evidence regarding hemoglobin A1c >8% was conflicting. Consensus supported individualized perioperative management of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis, alcohol-based skin preparation, and avoidance of razor shaving. Evidence was insufficient to determine the effects of testosterone supplementation, diagnostic indication, continuation of antiplatelet therapy before revision, extended oral antibiotic prophylaxis, or antibiotic prophylaxis for dental and other invasive procedures. Evidence was also insufficient to support specific intraoperative interventions for reducing PJI, including intrawound antibiotics, antiseptic irrigation, iodine-impregnated drapes, electrocautery, tranexamic acid, or selection of a particular arthroplasty type. CONCLUSION: The 2025 ICM identified several strategies applicable to current practice while highlighting substantial gaps in shoulder-specific evidence. Many recommendations remain based on limited or extrapolated evidence. Prospective shoulder-specific studies using clinical PJI as the primary outcome are needed to determine which prevention strategies provide meaningful benefit.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large RCT (60 patients) showing preemptive duloxetine does not reduce chronic postsurgical pain at 3 months post-THA, providing important negative evidence against a commonly proposed intervention for persistent pain prevention.
bullets: Male sex and clinical malnutrition are confirmed risk factors for periprosthetic shoulder infection, and corticosteroid injection within 3 months of shoulder arthroplasty should be avoided.

Alcohol-based skin prep, perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis, and individualized DMARD management are supported, while evidence is insufficient to recommend intrawound antibiotics, antiseptic irrigation, or iodine drapes.

Most shoulder PJI prevention recommendations are extrapolated from hip and knee data, meaning surgeons should treat current guidelines as provisional until shoulder-specific prospective studies are available.

candidates.title: Comparison of computed tomography-based tibial torsion measurement techniques reveals significant technique-dependent differences.
candidates.authors_short: Benefelds M, Juen U, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare commonly used computed tomography (CT)-based tibial torsion measurement discrepancies and evaluate their intra- and interobserver agreement, as measurement discrepancies between techniques have not been systematically assessed. METHODS: CT scans from 20 adult patients were retrospectively analysed. Tibial torsion was calculated using two proximal reference axes (posterior tibial plateau tangent and tibial tuberosity axis) and four distal axes (transmalleolar, ankle joint, Jend and Waidelich). Three observers performed all measurements independently and repeated them after 8-12 weeks. Differences among techniques were assessed using repeated-measures analysis of variance with Bonferroni correction. Reliability was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). RESULTS: All measurement techniques differed significantly (p < 0.05). Mean tibial torsion was 34.1° (standard deviation [SD] 8.6°) for the transmalleolar axis, 31.2° (SD 8.8°) for the ankle joint axis, 44.2° (SD 9.8°) for the Jend axis and 34.9° (SD 9.0°) for the Waidelich axis. Segmental values revealed a mean supratuberositary torsion of 26° (SD 6.7°) and a mean infratuberositary torsion of 7.9° (SD 8.8°) for the transmalleolar axis, 5.1° (SD 8.9°) for the ankle joint axis, 18.1° (SD 10.4°) for the Jend axis and 8.8° (SD 9.1°) for the Waidelich axis. All techniques showed excellent intra- and interobserver reliability (ICC > 0.89). CONCLUSION: Tibial torsion values depended strongly on the measurement technique used. Technique-specific normative values are essential, and radiology reports should explicitly identify the technique applied. Clinicians must account for these systematic differences when interpreting torsion values and planning derotational osteotomies. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective comparative study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Long-term study (1,140 TKAs, mean 20.5-year follow-up) demonstrating combined coronal and rotational malalignment independently predicts aseptic revision, reinforcing the importance of comprehensive alignment assessment.
bullets: CT-based tibial torsion measurements vary by up to 13 degrees depending on which proximal and distal reference axes are used, with the Jend axis consistently producing the highest values.
All techniques showed excellent reproducibility, so the variability comes from the method itself, not observer error.
Surgeons planning derotational osteotomies must confirm which measurement technique was used and apply normative values specific to that technique, not interchange values across methods.

candidates.title: Greater eccentric hamstrings to concentric quadriceps strength ratio at 6 months after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction is associated with reduced odds of revision within 2 years.
candidates.authors_short: Högberg J, Cristiani R, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To investigate the association between eccentric hamstrings-to-concentric quadriceps strength ratio (mixed hamstrings to quadriceps [HQ]-strength ratio) at 6 months postoperatively and revision anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACL-R) within 2 years of primary surgery. The secondary purpose was to investigate the association between the mixed HQ-strength ratio and single-leg hop for distance limb symmetry index (LSI). METHODS: Data were collected from a local registry at Capio Artro Clinic, Stockholm, Sweden. Patients aged ≥15 years, without concomitant ligament injuries and meniscal resection or repair who underwent primary ACL-R with hamstring tendon autografts between 2005 and 2021 were included. Isokinetic eccentric hamstrings and concentric quadriceps strength were assessed using a Biodex dynamometer 6 months postoperatively. Associations between mixed HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg and revision ACL-R were analysed using multivariable logistic regression analysis, presented with odds ratios (ORs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and area under the receiver operating characteristics curve (AUC). Associations between mixed HQ-strength ratio and single-leg hop for distance LSI were analysed with linear regression. RESULTS: Of the 3458 patients included, 49.5% were female and the mean age was 28.8 ± 10.4 years. Patients who underwent revision ACL-R within 2 years had lower mixed HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg 6 months postoperatively. After adjustment for age at primary ACL-R and preinjury Tegner level, each 10-unit increase in the mixed HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg was associated with lower odds of revision ACL-R (OR = 0.81, 95% CI [0.71;0.93], p = 0.003). However, the discriminatory ability was poor (AUC = 0.64). A greater mixed HQ-strength ratio was associated with poorer single-leg hop for distance LSI, adjusted for age at primary ACL-R and preinjury Tegner level (β = -1.30, 95% CI [-1.51;-1.09], p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: The mixed HQ-strength ratio may complement the evaluation of muscle strength recovery after ACL-R. However, its poor discriminatory ability limits its use to identify patients who will undergo revision ACL-R. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.
candidates.score_reasoning: Retrospective study (86 knees) demonstrating biplanar distal femoral osteotomy reduces lateral hinge fracture rate from 75% to 19% compared to monoplanar technique with equivalent coronal correction, a clinically actionable finding.
bullets: In over 3,400 patients after ACL reconstruction with hamstring autograft, a higher eccentric hamstring to concentric quadriceps strength ratio at 6 months was associated with lower odds of revision surgery within 2 years.
This finding applies to active patients aged 15 and older returning to sport after primary ACL reconstruction, particularly those being cleared at standard 6-month isokinetic testing.

The ratio adds useful information to routine strength assessments but cannot reliably identify individual patients at risk for revision, so it should complement, not replace, existing return-to-sport criteria.

Evidence is insufficient to recommend intrawound antibiotics, antiseptic irrigation, tranexamic acid, or extended oral antibiotics, so many hip and knee prevention strategies do not yet transfer to shoulder arthroplasty.
